prompt.context: Our client, Tarrant Fixtures, is a low-intensity manufacturing company that produces display fixtures for retail clients. The company's financial performance has deteriorated in each of the last three years. Specifically, they are concerned with the company's falling Return on Investment (ROI).
prompt.question: The CEO has asked us to look into this problem. How can Tarrant Fixtures get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What types of products does the company make?
clarifying_info.a: Two types: Custom displays (50% of sales) — produced only when an order is placed and payment is received. Standard displays (50% of sales) — manufactured to open standard sizes/types and stored in inventory (built-to-stock).

clarifying_info.q: How many standardized products does the company carry?
clarifying_info.a: Today there are 12 standardized products. Three years ago there were 5. The top 5 products still account for 80% of standardized product sales.

clarifying_info.q: How have revenues changed over the past three years?
clarifying_info.a: Total revenues grew 25%, from $100M to $125M, equally across both product types.
Costs of production (COGS, labor, SG&A, etc.) have remained stable as a percentage of revenue at 80%.

clarifying_info.q: Has the company made any new capital investments?
clarifying_info.a: No. There has been no new investment in Property, Plant, and Equipment (CAPEX = 0).

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to working capital?
clarifying_info.a: Total working capital employed three years ago was $80M; today it is $130M. Inventory levels increased 200%, from $25M to $75M, primarily in finished goods.
The market has grown 25% in total over the past three years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's market position?
clarifying_info.a: The client has remained the industry market share leader and has maintained 25% market share.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive environment like?
clarifying_info.a: There are several players in the market, but everything has remained stable from a competitive standpoint.

exhibits.title: Working Capital Statement
exhibits.shows: A line-by-line working capital statement listing categories of capital (inventory, AR, AP, cash, PP&E, etc.) for use in calculating Capital Employed and ROI.
exhibits.data: Working Capital Year 1: $80M total; Inventory Year 1: $25M. Working Capital Year 3: $130M total; Inventory Year 3: $75M.

framework: 1. Define ROI: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. Identify the two levers — net profit and capital employed.
2. Analyze Net Profit: Revenue trend vs. cost trend over the three-year period to determine whether profits are driving the ROI decline.
3. Analyze Capital Employed: Break down into PP&E and Working Capital; examine each sub-component (inventory, AR, AP, cash) for changes.
4. Identify root cause of capital increase: Drill into the inventory build-up and link it to the SKU proliferation in standardized products.
5. Develop recommendations to reduce inventory and restore ROI.

questions.prompt: Calculate Net Profit for Year 1 and Year 3. Is falling profit the cause of the ROI decline?
questions.guidance: The candidate should apply the 80% cost ratio to revenues. Net Profit Year 1 = $100M × 20% = $20M. Net Profit Year 3 = $125M × 20% = $25M. Profits grew 25% in absolute terms — the same rate as revenue — so declining profitability is NOT the cause of the ROI problem. The candidate should pivot to examine the denominator: Capital Employed.

math.setup: Net Profit = Revenue × (1 - Cost % of Revenue) = Revenue × 20%
steps: Change: +$5M (+25%) — profits grew proportionally with revenue
math.answer: Net Profit increased from $20M to $25M. Profit is not the source of the ROI decline.

questions.prompt: Examine Capital Employed using the working capital statement. What component is driving the increase?
questions.guidance: PP&E is constant (no CAPEX). Total working capital increased by $50M (from $80M to $130M). The candidate should note that the $50M increase in working capital equals the $50M increase in inventory (from $25M to $75M, a 200% increase). All other items — AR, AP, cash — are stable. Inventory is the culprit.

math.setup: Change in Capital Employed = Change in Working Capital = Change in Inventory (since PP&E and all other WC items are stable)
steps: Working Capital Year 1: $80M; Year 3: $130M → increase of $50M
All other WC items are stable → 100% of WC increase is attributable to inventory
math.answer: Capital Employed increased by $50M, entirely due to inventory build-up.

questions.prompt: Calculate ROI for Year 1 and Year 3 and confirm the decline.
questions.guidance: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. Year 1: $20M / $80M = 25%. Year 3: $25M / $130M ≈ 19.2%. ROI declined by approximately 5.8 percentage points despite profit growth, confirming the issue is in the denominator.

math.answer: ROI fell from ~25% to ~19.2%, a decline of ~5.8 pp, driven by the $50M inventory increase.

questions.prompt: Why has inventory increased so dramatically? What are the root causes?
questions.guidance: The candidate should connect the data point that standard SKUs grew from 5 to 12. Since standard products are built-to-stock, more SKUs means more finished goods to hold. Strong answers will also surface: (1) inaccurate demand forecasts leading to excess safety stock, and (2) obsolete inventory from discontinued or slow-moving SKU variants. Note that the top 5 products still generate 80% of standard product sales — the 7 new SKUs represent significant inventory risk with low sales volume.

brainstorming.prompt: What can management do to reduce inventory and restore ROI?

categories.name: Rationalize the product line
ideas: Reduce the standard product line from 12 SKUs back down to the top 5 (which drive 80% of standard sales)
Institute a product portfolio review process to gate future SKU additions
Require minimum volume thresholds before a new standard SKU is added to the catalog

categories.name: Improve demand forecasting
ideas: Implement statistical demand forecasting to set data-driven safety stock levels
Collaborate with retail clients on forward order visibility / vendor-managed inventory
Use sales history from the top-5 SKUs as benchmarks for new SKU ramp-up assumptions

categories.name: Reduce obsolete and excess inventory
ideas: Identify and write off obsolete inventory (accept the one-time profit hit to clean the balance sheet)
Run promotional discounts or clearance programs to work down slow-moving SKUs
Explore return-to-vendor or liquidation channels for excess finished goods

categories.name: Process and operational improvements
ideas: Shift more standard SKUs to a build-to-order or postponement model where feasible
Shorten manufacturing lead times so less safety stock is needed
Implement pull-based replenishment (e.g., kanban) for standard product lines

recommendation: Tarrant Fixtures' ROI has declined from ~25% to ~19% over three years because a $50M inventory build-up inflated Capital Employed, even as profits grew 25%.
The immediate priority is to reduce standard product SKUs from 12 back to the top 5 (which account for 80% of standard product revenue) and write off or work down obsolete inventory.
In parallel, the company should invest in demand forecasting capabilities to set accurate safety stock levels and prevent future inventory over-build.
risks: Writing off obsolete inventory will cause an immediate one-time hit to net profits, so management may resist; phased clearance may be more politically viable.
Reducing SKUs could disappoint some retail clients who order the 7 marginal products; the company should validate demand before eliminating lines.
Without a governance process for new SKU additions, product proliferation may recur as the sales team responds to one-off customer requests.
next_steps: Conduct a full inventory audit to quantify obsolete vs. excess vs. active finished goods by SKU.
Model the P&L impact of a write-off vs. a clearance/sell-through approach for obsolete stock.
Pilot improved demand forecasting (statistical + customer collaboration) for the top-5 standard SKUs.
Establish a formal SKU governance policy with a cross-functional review committee before committing to future standard product additions.
